title: The 7 Most Counter-Intuitive Teaching Ideas I Have Learnt
author: Dario Emanuele Source: dremanuele.substack.com
summary: Drawing on a decade in the classroom and research from Craig Barton, Kris Boulton, and Ollie Lovell, Dario Emanuele identifies seven counter-intuitive teaching shifts that transformed his practice. The seven: (1) Stop designing slides and rehearse explanations instead — teacher presence and clarity drive learning, not slide transitions; (2) The visualiser is the most powerful classroom tool, forcing the teacher to slow to the student's pace and model the 'messy' reality of thinking in real time; (3) Behaviour policies require principled professional judgment, not rigid scripts — especially with high-trauma or high-SEN students; (4) The lesson plan is a hypothesis — pivot immediately when foundational knowledge is missing; (5) Behaviour is the prerequisite for the lesson, not one of many standards — teach it like a subject, reset when needed; (6) For low-independence classes, 'revision' should become re-teaching with I Do / We Do / You Do, not self-directed worksheets; (7) Physical manipulatives in whole-class settings create cognitive load problems — use pictorial representations on the visualiser instead, reserving manipulatives for 1:1 or SEN work.
points: Slide design time is misallocated planning energy: hours spent on fonts and animations trade away time that should go to practicing explanations, anticipating misconceptions, and refining I-Do scripts — the teacher's presence and clarity are the primary learning drivers.

Live-modeling on a visualiser forces teachers to slow to the pace of a student's pen, models the messy reality of thinking (crossing out, adjusting), and turns a static presentation into a dynamic masterclass — almost every I Do / We Do / You Do sequence is better delivered this way than via digital slides.

When a class can't access the day's content because foundational knowledge is missing, pivoting immediately to close that gap is the correct move — a 'messy detour' that secures foundations beats a 'perfect' plan that leaves 80% of the class behind.

Behaviour must be taught like a subject: if students can't meet behavioural norms, stop the curriculum, reset, reteach the norms, and restart — the scheme-of-work deficit is worth accepting to preserve the conditions for actual learning.

Concrete manipulatives in whole-class settings often teach students how to use the tool rather than the underlying concept; pictorial representations on the visualiser are cleaner, cheaper, and keep cognitive focus on the concept.
quotes: True expertise isn't about adding more; it's about stripping away the fluff to find the 'silver bullets' that actually move the needle.

Spend your planning time practicing your explanations, anticipating misconceptions, and refining your 'I Do' scripts. Your presence and clarity are the primary drivers of learning, not your slide transitions.
A 'perfect' lesson plan that leaves 80% of the class behind is a failure. A 'messy' detour that secures foundational knowledge is definitely better.

Behaviour isn't a 'part' of the lesson; it is the pre-requisite for the lesson. If they can't do it, stop the curriculum and 'teach behaviour' again. Reset, restart, and repeat. You might be 'behind' on the scheme of work, but you will be miles ahead in actual learning.
If your students lack the metacognition to self-direct their revision or reflect on their results, don't force it. Transform 'revision' or 'feedback' back into 'teaching.'
